newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end lower before 5-yr T-note auction.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end lower before 5-yr T-note auction.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended lower for the third straight day on Wednesday after a disappointing two-year Treasury note auction prompted players to cut prices before Thursday's five-year Treasury note sale.

"The two-year auction was supposed to be the easier of the two sales and demand wasn't particularly strong, so there's concern about how Thursday's auction will go," said Michelle Laughlin, Treasury market strategist at Prudential Securities. "People are positioning themselves. They're backing the market up for a concession ahead of the auction."
Dealers hope that lower prices will attract more bidders to the auction and facilitate the distribution of the new securities.
The Treasury sold $18.25 billion in its monthly auction of two-year notes on Wednesday and is scheduled to sell $12.5 billion in five-year notes on Thursday.
The Treasury market opened slightly higher in thin morning trade but slipped into the minus column right after the early afternoon bidding deadline for the two-year notes.
Prices hovered at those slightly lower levels for a little over an hour.
Then, reacting to the two-year auction results announced by the Treasury, prices tread a downward path.
The Treasury said it sold the notes at a 5.874 percent yield. One positive aspect of the auction was that non-competitive bids totaled $1.34 billion.

"That was the best since September and certainly stronger than the $928 million in non-competitive bids you had in November," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market analyst at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. On the other hand, the 2.23 bid-to-cover ratio was weaker than the average 2.58 bid-to-cover ratio for two-year note sales, he said.

"Event risk" -- that the market must absorb three new economic reports before the 1300 EST/1800 GMT bidding deadline for Thursday's Treasury auction -- contributed to dealers' inclination to cut prices before the five-year note sale, analysts said. The market gets weekly jobless claims figures, monthly trade figures and the Philadelphia Federal Reserve survey on Thursday morning.
"The two-year auction didn't go that well and on top of that you're expecting some stronger economic news," said Laughlin. "That combination suggested that the five-year auction might be difficult."
In thin trade, the market also experienced some technical deterioration.
"The March futures contract closed below 112-08 which had been considered a critical, pivotal support level," said Laughlin.
March T-bonds closed at 112-02 in Chicago.
A close at 111 even would mark a 50 percent retracement of the rally that began on September 5, Laughlin said.
In the cash market, the 6-1/2-percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended at 97-12/32, down 16/32, its yield up to 6.70 percent versus 6.66 percent at Tuesday's close.
Two-year notes fell 3/32 to 99-15/32, yielding 5.92 percent. Five-year notes dropped 5/32 to 98-18/32 to yield 6.22 percent. Ten-year notes skidded 10/32 to 100-8/32 to end with a 6.46 percent yield.
Three-month bill rates fell one basis point to 4.89 percent, six-month bill rates rose one basis point to 5.08 percent and year bill rates rose three basis points to 5.26 percent.
